plan.chapter_thesis: Training optical diffractive neural networks requires adapting gradient-based optimization to the physical reality of diffraction, where the choice of loss function, differentiability assumptions, and regularization strategy critically determines whether the resulting network is computationally effective and physically realizable.
plan.reader_takeaway: Successful ODNN training depends not just on backpropagation through the diffraction integral, but on physics-aware strategies like hardware-in-the-loop optimization and fabrication-tolerant regularizers that bridge the simulation-to-reality gap.

argument_sequence.purpose: Establish the fundamental mechanism of end-to-end differentiable training through the physical diffraction model.
Demonstrate the computational advantages and all-optical inference capabilities enabled by this training paradigm.
Address the simulation-to-reality gap and the necessity of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) training methodologies.
Explain physics-informed optimization strategies that incorporate fabrication constraints and spectral properties directly into the loss landscape.
Explore alternative and hybrid training frameworks that address non-differentiable components or reduce complexity.
Illustrate advanced multiplexing and reconfigurability techniques enabled by specific training approaches.
Synthesize the scalability of these paradigms to complex, real-world tasks beyond simple classification.

terminology_rows.note: Backpropagation through the scalar diffraction integral to optimize phase profiles.
Integrating the physical optical setup directly into the optimization loop to correct for misalignments and aberrations.
Incorporating physical constraints like dispersion formulas and fabrication tolerances into the loss function.
The performance discrepancy between idealized numerical models and physical hardware implementations.
Implementing the backpropagation algorithm directly within the optical system rather than in digital simulation.

explanation_block_rows.title: Foundations of Differentiable Optical Training
explanation_block_rows.goal: Define the core mechanism of treating optical propagation as a differentiable computational graph for gradient descent.

explanation_block_rows.title: Computational Advantages of All-Optical Inference
explanation_block_rows.goal: Quantify the speed and energy efficiency gains resulting from parallel optical propagation trained via these methods.

explanation_block_rows.title: Bridging the Simulation-to-Reality Gap
explanation_block_rows.goal: Analyze the limitations of pure simulation and the role of Hardware-In-the-Loop (HIL) training in correcting physical errors.

explanation_block_rows.title: Physics-Aware Regularization and Inverse Design
explanation_block_rows.goal: Detail how fabrication constraints and spectral dispersion are embedded into the optimization objective to ensure realizability.

explanation_block_rows.title: Alternative and Hybrid Training Paradigms
explanation_block_rows.goal: Evaluate non-standard approaches like in situ backpropagation and hybrid electronic-optical training for handling non-differentiable elements.

explanation_block_rows.title: Multiplexing and Reconfigurable Architectures
explanation_block_rows.goal: Showcase how training enables multi-functional networks through polarization and wavelength multiplexing.

explanation_block_rows.title: Scalability to Complex Real-World Tasks
explanation_block_rows.goal: Demonstrate the extension of these training methods to high-dimensional problems like segmentation, sensing, and imaging through unknown media.
